analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas drilling off the California coast.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal law to permanently prohibit oil and gas preleasing and leasing in federal waters off the coast of California. It would also exclude those waters from a government-mandated inventory of offshore oil and gas resources. Existing leases issued before enactment would keep their rights, but no new drilling areas could be opened.
analysis.who_benefits: California coastal residents, tourism businesses, and fisheries, whose shoreline would be protected from new offshore drilling platforms, construction, and the risk of oil spills. Taxpayers would also avoid subsidizing a government inventory aimed at opening new offshore acreage.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in all areas of the Outer Continental Shelf off the coast of California, permanently and notwithstanding any other law [S2][S3].

Excludes California's offshore waters from the comprehensive inventory and analysis of Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas resources required by the Energy Policy Act of 2005, keeping them out of the pipeline for future lease sales [S2][S3].
Existing leases issued before the bill's enactment would retain their rights, so the ban targets new drilling activity without disrupting in-place operations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that would have sought new leases off California lose access to those waters. Federal and state revenues from future offshore lease sales in the region would go uncollected. Consumers nationwide would forgo whatever oil and gas might have been produced from those waters, though the amounts were never inventoried.

drawbacks.text: The ban locks up whatever oil and natural gas lies beneath California's federal offshore waters, reducing domestic energy supply and the lease revenues drilling would generate — costs that fall diffusely on energy consumers and taxpayers [S2][S3].

A state-by-state prohibition is piecemeal: the same bill leaves drilling open in other regions' federal waters, so protections depend on each state assembling its own legislation rather than on a national standard [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Californians the benefit is concrete and localized — no new drilling platforms, construction traffic, or spill risk along their coast — while the cost is spread thinly across the nation as foregone energy supply and revenue. The main design weakness is that it protects one state's coast by statute rather than establishing a broader standard for other offshore areas facing the same pressure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which took no further action on it, and it died there when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer, joined by Senator Dianne Feinstein, introduced the bill in the Senate on February 16, 2006 [S1][S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote after referral; the only later entry is a second set of the sponsor's introductory remarks on March 9, 2006 [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and bills not reported out of committee expire with the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies remain free to press for drilling access off California, which stays open to future leasing under existing law, while no one gained the coastal protections the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks twice, in February and March 2006.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, introduced for herself and Senator Boxer.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape cannot be measured — though the Republican-chaired committee of referral never moved it.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar new leasing off California, closing one of the industry's most potentially valuable untapped offshore areas and removing it from the federal resource-inventory process. Offshore drilling carries spill risks borne by coastal residents and tourism economies, so the industry's interest runs against the public's on this stretch of water.

Blocking new drilling platforms off the coast protects the beaches, fisheries, and recreation that draw visitors and sustain fishing businesses. Their gain comes directly from the protection the public also gets.
